byzanz#consequences.4: Icons, domed churches and gold mosaics in the Byzantine tradition shape the art of the Orthodox world, and the Hagia Sophia also influenced the great mosques of the Ottomans.
byzanz#consequences.5: The split between the Eastern and Western churches and the sack of Constantinople in 1204 still weigh on relations between Catholic and Orthodox Christians today.
byzanz#keyFacts.0: In 330 Constantine the Great dedicates Constantinople as his new capital; in 395 the empire is divided into a western and an eastern half.
byzanz#keyFacts.1: Justinian I has Roman law compiled in 529–534, dedicates the Hagia Sophia in 537 and reconquers North Africa and Italy.
byzanz#keyFacts.2: In 636 the Byzantine army is defeated by the Arabs at the Yarmuk; Syria, Palestine and Egypt are lost.
byzanz#keyFacts.3: In 726 or 730 the Iconoclast controversy begins under Leo III; it ends only in 843 with the final restoration of the veneration of images.
byzanz#keyFacts.4: In 863 Cyril and Methodius set out on their mission to the Slavs in Great Moravia; in 1014 Basil II defeats the Bulgarians at the Kleidion pass.
byzanz#keyFacts.5: In 1054 papal legates and the patriarch of Constantinople excommunicate each other; in 1071 the Seljuks win at Manzikert.
byzanz#keyFacts.6: In 1204 crusaders sack Constantinople; in 1261 Michael VIII Palaiologos recovers the city, which falls to the Ottomans in 1453.
byzanz#sections.0.title: Rule and Politics
byzanz#sections.0.paragraphs.0: At the head of the empire stood the emperor, in Greek basileus, who saw himself as the successor of the Roman emperors and as a ruler appointed by God over the Christian world. There was no fixed rule of succession: an emperor was legitimate if he was acknowledged by the senate, the army and the people and, as a rule, crowned by the patriarch. Many emperors rose as generals or courtiers; others were overthrown, blinded or banished to monasteries. Dynasties such as the Macedonians, the Komnenoi and the Palaiologoi tried to keep the throne in the family through co-emperors and marriage alliances.
byzanz#sections.0.paragraphs.1: The empire was governed from Constantinople by a large administration that worked in writing and was headed by high palace dignitaries. From the 7th century the empire was divided into themes, military districts in which a commander also took on civil duties; how and when this system arose is debated among historians. Diplomacy was one of the emperors' strengths: they negotiated with gold, titles, lavish receptions and marriages, played neighbouring peoples off against each other and bound foreign princes to themselves through baptism and honorary titles.
byzanz#sections.0.paragraphs.2: The empire was almost constantly threatened on several fronts: in the east by Persians, Arabs and later Seljuks, in the north by Avars, Bulgarians and Rus, in the west by Normans and crusaders. Alongside the armies of the themes, mercenaries played a growing role, among them the Varangian Guard of Scandinavians and Rus. From the 11th century great aristocratic families gained power, and the emperors granted revenues from land, the pronoia, in return for military service. After 1204, and above all in the Palaiologan period, civil wars and dependence on Venice and Genoa decisively weakened the empire.
byzanz#sections.1.title: Society and Everyday Life
byzanz#sections.1.paragraphs.0: For centuries Constantinople was one of the largest and richest cities in the world; in the 6th century it had, by estimates, several hundred thousand inhabitants. Public life took place in churches, in markets and in the Hippodrome, where chariot races were held and the people could cheer or jeer the emperor. The circus factions of the Blues and the Greens were both fan clubs and political groups. The great majority of the population, however, lived as peasants in villages, paid taxes and supplied soldiers.
byzanz#sections.1.paragraphs.1: Society was shaped by Christianity but was multilingual: alongside Greeks, Armenians, Syrians, Slavs, Jews and many others lived in the empire, and people from all these groups could rise in the army and administration. Churches, monasteries and endowments maintained hospitals, poorhouses and orphanages. Monasteries owned large estates and monks enjoyed great prestige; from the 10th century Mount Athos became the centre of Orthodox monasticism.
byzanz#sections.1.paragraphs.2: Women were legally subordinate to men but could own property and inherit, and in the upper class some wielded great power. Empresses such as Theodora, Irene, who in 797 even ruled alone as emperor, and Zoe helped shape politics, and in the 12th century Anna Komnene wrote an important work of history. Education was more widespread in the city than in the medieval West; officials, clergy and many merchants could read and write.
byzanz#sections.2.title: Culture, Religion and Knowledge
byzanz#sections.2.paragraphs.0: Christianity was the foundation of the empire. Emperors summoned the great councils at which the doctrine of Christ was defined, for example at Chalcedon in 451; those who rejected their decisions, like many Christians in Egypt and Syria, were regarded as dissenters. Church and emperor were closely linked, but the Iconoclast controversy showed that monks and bishops could also stand up to the ruler. Over time the Greek church and the Latin church of Rome grew apart over questions such as papal primacy and the Filioque in the Creed.
byzanz#sections.2.paragraphs.1: Byzantine art served above all the faith. Icons, painted images of Christ, Mary and the saints, were venerated and seen as windows onto the heavenly world. Gold-ground mosaics in the Hagia Sophia, in Ravenna, in Thessaloniki or in the Chora Church in Constantinople display a solemn, otherworldly visual language. The domed church on a cross-shaped plan became the model for churches from Venice to Kyiv.
byzanz#sections.2.paragraphs.2: Byzantium preserved the learning of antiquity: scholars copied and commented on the works of Homer, Plato, Aristotle and the Greek physicians and mathematicians, and many ancient texts survive only in Byzantine manuscripts. Historians such as Procopius, Michael Psellos and Anna Komnene continued the classical tradition. In the 14th and 15th centuries scholars such as Manuel Chrysoloras and Bessarion brought the Greek language and Greek books to Italy and thus contributed to Renaissance humanism.
byzanz#sections.3.title: Economy and Technology
byzanz#sections.3.paragraphs.0: The gold coin known as the solidus, in Greek nomisma, introduced by Constantine the Great, remained stable until the 11th century and was sought after throughout the Mediterranean. Only in the 11th century was its gold content sharply reduced, until Alexios I Komnenos created a new gold coin, the hyperpyron, in 1092. The state collected taxes mainly from the rural population, levied duties on trade and used them to fund the army, administration, building projects and tribute payments to neighbours.
byzanz#sections.3.paragraphs.1: Constantinople lay at the crossroads of trade routes between the Black Sea and the Mediterranean, Europe and Asia. Silk was especially valuable: according to Procopius, silkworms reached the empire under Justinian, and imperial workshops produced precious fabrics whose export was strictly controlled. The Book of the Eparch from the 10th century laid down how the guilds of silk merchants, goldsmiths and bakers were allowed to operate. From the 11th century Venice, and later Pisa and Genoa, received trading privileges that harmed the empire's own merchants.
byzanz#sections.3.paragraphs.2: In technology the Byzantines impressed with structures such as the dome of the Hagia Sophia, the Theodosian Walls and the cisterns that supplied Constantinople with water. In war they gained an advantage at sea from Greek fire, an incendiary weapon whose exact composition was kept secret and remains unknown to this day. Military manuals such as the Strategikon described tactics, siegecraft and how to deal with different enemies.
wikinger-nordeuropa#summary: From the raid on Lindisfarne in 793 to the Kalmar Union of 1397, the peoples of Scandinavia appeared as raiders, traders and settlers between North America and Byzantium, became Christian and formed the kingdoms of Denmark, Norway and Sweden.
wikinger-nordeuropa#overview.0: At the end of the 8th century Denmark, Norway and Sweden were home to farming communities under chieftains and petty kings, linked to the rest of Europe by seafaring and trade. The raid on the monastery of Lindisfarne in 793 opened the Viking Age, in which Scandinavian seafarers struck coasts and rivers from Ireland to the Mediterranean. Why the raids began just then is debated: historians point to the wealth of unprotected monasteries and trading places, power struggles at home that sent young men in search of loot and renown, possibly a shortage of land, and above all the fast, seaworthy longship.
wikinger-nordeuropa#overview.1: In the 9th century isolated raids turned into campaigns and land-taking. Vikings sacked Paris in 845, founded the base of Dublin in Ireland in 841, and from 865 the Great Heathen Army conquered most of the Anglo-Saxon kingdoms. Only Wessex under Alfred the Great held out; eastern England was settled by Scandinavians as the Danelaw. In 911 the West Frankish king Charles the Simple ceded the area around Rouen to the leader Rollo, and Normandy grew out of it.
wikinger-nordeuropa#overview.2: At the same time Scandinavians sailed across the North Atlantic. From about 870 they settled Iceland, where in 930 the Althing emerged as a common assembly. Erik the Red led settlers to Greenland around 985, and his son Leif Eriksson reached North America around 1000; the site of L’Anse aux Meadows in Newfoundland confirms the sagas’ accounts of Norse voyages to America. In the east, Swedish Varangians travelled the Russian rivers as far as Byzantium and the Caliphate and contributed to the rise of Kievan Rus.
wikinger-nordeuropa#overview.3: In the 10th and 11th centuries the kingdoms of Denmark, Norway and Sweden became more solid and Christian. Harald Bluetooth boasted on the Jelling runestone that he had made the Danes Christian, Olaf Tryggvason and Saint Olaf imposed Christianity in Norway, and Iceland adopted it around 1000 by decision of the Althing. Around 1028 Cnut the Great ruled England, Denmark and Norway in a North Sea Empire. When the Norwegian king Harald Hardrada fell at Stamford Bridge in 1066, the age of the great Viking expeditions ended; not quite three weeks later the Norman William won at Hastings.
wikinger-nordeuropa#overview.4: In the High and Late Middle Ages the Nordic kingdoms came to resemble the rest of Europe, with archbishoprics, monasteries, castles and towns. In Iceland scholars such as Snorri Sturluson wrote down sagas and the Edda, and in 1262 the island submitted to the Norwegian king. Baltic trade was dominated by the German Hanseatic League, with which Denmark went to war after taking Visby in 1361 and had to conclude the Peace of Stralsund in 1370. In 1397 Queen Margaret I united Denmark, Norway and Sweden in the Kalmar Union, which lasted until 1523.
wikinger-nordeuropa#consequences.0: The Vikings changed the map of Europe: Dublin, Normandy, the Danelaw in England and the settlements in Iceland and the Faroes go back to their raids and land-taking.
wikinger-nordeuropa#consequences.1: The Normans, descendants of the Vikings in Normandy, conquered England in 1066 and southern Italy and Sicily in the 11th century, shaping the history of western Europe and the Mediterranean.
wikinger-nordeuropa#consequences.2: Iceland’s Althing is regarded as one of the oldest assemblies in Europe; the names of parliaments such as the Norwegian Storting and the Danish Folketing still go back to the thing.
wikinger-nordeuropa#consequences.3: The Icelandic sagas, the Edda and the runestones are the most important sources on the Norse gods and continue to shape literature, music, films and games today.
wikinger-nordeuropa#consequences.4: L’Anse aux Meadows proves that Europeans were in America some 500 years before Columbus, even though the settlement was short-lived and had no lasting consequences.
wikinger-nordeuropa#consequences.5: The Kalmar Union and its break-up laid the foundations of the later states of Denmark, Norway and Sweden, whose close ties still show today in Nordic cooperation.
wikinger-nordeuropa#keyFacts.0: In 793 Vikings raid the monastery of Lindisfarne; in 845 they sack Paris.
wikinger-nordeuropa#keyFacts.1: In 865 the Great Heathen Army lands in England; after Alfred’s victory at Edington in 878 the Danelaw takes shape.
wikinger-nordeuropa#keyFacts.2: In 911 Rollo receives the land around Rouen, the core of Normandy, from Charles the Simple.
wikinger-nordeuropa#keyFacts.3: In 930 the Althing meets for the first time in Iceland; around 1000 the island adopts Christianity.
wikinger-nordeuropa#keyFacts.4: Around 985 Erik the Red settles Greenland; around 1000 Leif Eriksson reaches Vinland in North America.
wikinger-nordeuropa#keyFacts.5: In 1016 Cnut the Great becomes king of England; in 1066 Harald Hardrada falls at Stamford Bridge.
wikinger-nordeuropa#keyFacts.6: In 1370 the Hanseatic League secures its privileges in the Peace of Stralsund; in 1397 the Kalmar Union is formed under Margaret I.
wikinger-nordeuropa#sections.0.title: Rule and Politics
wikinger-nordeuropa#sections.0.paragraph: In the early Viking Age Scandinavia had many petty kings, jarls and chieftains whose power rested on followers, land and plunder. A leader had to bind his warriors to him with gifts, feasts and shares of the loot; whoever was successful attracted more men. Important decisions were taken at the thing, the assembly of free men, which administered justice, settled disputes and acknowledged kings. In Iceland, which had no king, the Althing became the island’s highest authority from 930.

From the 10th century royal families established themselves in Denmark, Norway and Sweden, unified the land and promoted Christianity. Harald Bluetooth had ring fortresses and bridges built in Denmark, Cnut the Great ruled England, Denmark and Norway for a time, and in Norway Olaf Haraldsson was revered after his death in 1030 as the country’s eternal king. Disputes over the throne nevertheless remained frequent, especially in Norway, where long civil wars raged in the 12th century.

In the High and Late Middle Ages the kings, with the help of the Church, expanded administration, laws and taxes and struggled with the nobility for power. Iceland and Greenland submitted to the Norwegian king between 1261 and 1264. Through marriages and inheritances the royal houses grew together, until in 1397 Margaret I united the three realms in the Kalmar Union under her great-nephew Eric of Pomerania; the union finally broke apart in 1523, when Sweden left under Gustav Vasa.
wikinger-nordeuropa#sections.1.title: Society and Everyday Life
wikinger-nordeuropa#sections.1.paragraph: Most people in the North were farmers who grew grain, kept livestock, fished and hunted on single farmsteads or in small villages. Society was roughly divided into chieftains and nobles, free farmers who were entitled to bear arms and attend the thing, and the unfree, the thralls. Slaves were an important prize of Viking raids and were sold at markets such as Hedeby, Dublin or on the Volga. Family and honour mattered greatly; disputes were often settled by compensation payments, but could also turn into long blood feuds.

Women ran the household economy, held the keys as a sign of their status and could own property, inherit and divorce. Rich graves such as the Oseberg ship burial in Norway show the high standing of some women. How far women themselves took part in raids is debated; DNA analysis of a richly furnished warrior grave from Birka has revived the discussion. Most Scandinavians never left home, but tens of thousands emigrated to England, Ireland, Iceland or Normandy.
wikinger-nordeuropa#sections.2.title: Culture, Religion and Knowledge
wikinger-nordeuropa#sections.2.paragraph: Before Christianization the Scandinavians worshipped many gods such as Odin, Thor, Freyr and Freyja, made sacrifices and buried the dead with grave goods, sometimes in ships. What we know of this world of gods comes mainly from Christian sources of the 13th century, above all the Edda, and must therefore be read with caution. Writing was done in runes, whose younger row had 16 signs; thousands of runestones commemorate the dead and voyages to England or the East.

Christianization took around three centuries. After early missions such as that of Ansgar in Birka around 830, the kings converted in the 10th and 11th centuries and imposed the faith from above. In 1103 or 1104 Lund received an archbishopric of its own for the North, later followed by Nidaros (Trondheim) and Uppsala. The Church brought the Latin alphabet, monasteries and schools; in Iceland a unique literature in the vernacular arose in the 13th century, including the sagas of Icelanders and the kings’ histories of Snorri Sturluson.
wikinger-nordeuropa#sections.3.title: Economy and Technology
wikinger-nordeuropa#sections.3.paragraph: The basis of their success was the longship: a slender, clinker-built boat with a keel, square sail and oars that could cross the open sea and, thanks to its shallow draught, penetrate far up rivers. Alongside it there were broader cargo ships such as the knarr, in which settlers brought livestock and supplies to Iceland and Greenland. Finds such as the Oseberg and Gokstad ships or the Skuldelev ships from Roskilde Fjord show the shipbuilding skill of the age.

The Vikings were not only raiders but also traders. Markets such as Hedeby, Birka and Kaupang linked western Europe with the East, through which furs, amber, walrus ivory and slaves were exchanged for silver, silk and wine. Tens of thousands of Arab silver coins in hoards, especially on Gotland, attest to trade with the Caliphate. Silver was often traded by weight and hacked into pieces for the purpose; in addition, English and Frankish rulers paid large tributes, the Danegeld.

In the High and Late Middle Ages the German Hanseatic League, with its cogs, took over long-distance trade in the Baltic. Visby on Gotland was an early centre, Hanseatic merchants maintained a kontor in Bergen for the stockfish trade, and the herring fishery off Scania was one of the region’s most important businesses. Dependence on Hanseatic trade led to conflicts with the Nordic kings, above all with Valdemar IV of Denmark.
russland-osteuropa#summary: From Kievan Rus by way of the Golden Horde, the rise of Moscow and the dual commonwealth of Poland-Lithuania to the tsarist empire of the Romanovs, East Slavic, Baltic and Polish states shaped the east of Europe for more than a thousand years, until the February Revolution of 1917 brought the monarchy to an end.
russland-osteuropa#overview.0: In the 9th century Kievan Rus took shape along the rivers between the Baltic and the Black Sea. According to the tradition of the Primary Chronicle, the Varangian Rurik was invited to Novgorod in 862; his follower Oleg made Kyiv, around 882, the centre of a loose realm of Scandinavian warriors and Slavic tribes that lived from trade with Byzantium. Princess Olga was baptized in Constantinople, her grandson Volodymyr made Orthodox Christianity the religion of the Rus in 988, and under Yaroslav the Wise Kyiv flourished with St Sophia's Cathedral and the law code known as the Russkaya Pravda. The Rus is regarded as the common root of Ukraine, Russia and Belarus.
russland-osteuropa#overview.1: After Yaroslav's death in 1054 the Rus broke up into rival principalities such as Vladimir-Suzdal, Galicia-Volhynia and the city republic of Novgorod. Between 1237 and 1240 the Mongols under Batu conquered most of them and destroyed Kyiv; the princes had to pay tribute to the Golden Horde on the Volga and have their rule confirmed by the khan. Novgorod was spared, and its prince Alexander Nevsky fought off the Swedes in 1240 and the Livonian Order in 1242. In the 14th century the western lands of the Rus passed to the rising Grand Duchy of Lithuania and to Poland.
russland-osteuropa#overview.2: Moscow, an insignificant place in the 13th century, became the seat of the metropolitan and the Horde's tax collector under Ivan I Kalita. Dmitry Donskoy defeated an army of the Horde on the field of Kulikovo in 1380, and Ivan III subdued Novgorod, ended dependence on the Tatars after the Great Stand on the Ugra in 1480 and called himself sovereign of all Rus. In the west, Poland and Lithuania joined in the Union of Krewo in 1385, defeated the Teutonic Order at Grunwald in 1410 and in 1569 merged in the Union of Lublin into the Commonwealth of the Two Nations, a nobles' state with an elected king.
russland-osteuropa#overview.3: Ivan IV was crowned tsar in 1547, conquered Kazan and Astrakhan and spread terror in his own country with the oprichnina. After his dynasty died out, famine, struggles for the throne and foreign armies plunged the realm into the Time of Troubles, until an assembly of the land elected Michael Romanov in 1613. The Cossacks of Ukraine rose against Poland-Lithuania under Bohdan Khmelnytsky in 1648 and placed themselves under the tsar in 1654. Peter the Great defeated Sweden at Poltava in 1709, founded St Petersburg and rebuilt state and army on Western models; Catherine the Great won the Crimea and, together with Prussia and Austria, partitioned Poland-Lithuania between 1772 and 1795, which vanished from the map despite the Constitution of 3 May 1791.
russland-osteuropa#overview.4: In the 19th century the tsarist empire stretched from Poland to the Pacific and for a time as far as Alaska. In the Decembrist revolt of 1825 officers demanded a constitution, Poland rose in vain in 1830 and 1863, and defeat in the Crimean War led to the abolition of serfdom under Alexander II in 1861. Industry and railways grew, while the state intensified the Russification of Poles, Ukrainians, Lithuanians and Belarusians and discrimination against Jews. The Revolution of 1905 forced the creation of a parliament, the Duma; in the First World War the monarchy lost its support, and in March 1917 Nicholas II abdicated.
russland-osteuropa#consequences.0: Ukrainians, Russians and Belarusians all trace their history back to Kievan Rus; who owns its legacy remains a politically contested question to this day.
russland-osteuropa#consequences.1: Orthodox Christianity, the Cyrillic alphabet and church architecture from Byzantium shape the culture of the East Slavic countries to the present.
russland-osteuropa#consequences.2: The experience of the partitions and uprisings made the Constitution of 3 May 1791 and the struggle for freedom pillars of Polish and Lithuanian national identity.
russland-osteuropa#consequences.3: Expansion across Siberia to the Pacific created the largest state on earth and a multi-ethnic empire whose borders and minority questions still have effects today.
russland-osteuropa#consequences.4: The late abolition of serfdom and rural poverty burdened Russia into the 20th century and prepared the ground for the revolutions of 1905 and 1917.
russland-osteuropa#consequences.5: The literature, music and painting of the 19th century, from Pushkin and Shevchenko to Tolstoy and Tchaikovsky, became a lasting part of world culture.
russland-osteuropa#keyFacts.0: In 862, according to the Primary Chronicle, the Varangian Rurik is invited to Novgorod; around 882 Oleg makes Kyiv the centre of the Rus.
russland-osteuropa#keyFacts.1: In 988 Grand Prince Volodymyr is baptized; under Yaroslav the Wise (1019–1054) the Russkaya Pravda is compiled.
russland-osteuropa#keyFacts.2: In 1237–1240 the Mongols conquer the Rus and destroy Kyiv; in 1380 Dmitry Donskoy wins on the field of Kulikovo.
russland-osteuropa#keyFacts.3: In 1480 the Great Stand on the Ugra ends the Golden Horde's rule over Moscow; in 1547 Ivan IV is crowned tsar.
russland-osteuropa#keyFacts.4: In 1569 Poland and Lithuania unite in the Union of Lublin; in 1613 an assembly of the land elects Michael Romanov tsar.
russland-osteuropa#keyFacts.5: In 1648 the Cossacks rise under Khmelnytsky; in 1703 Peter the Great founds St Petersburg, and in 1709 he wins at Poltava.
russland-osteuropa#keyFacts.6: In 1772–1795 Poland-Lithuania is partitioned three times; in 1861 Alexander II abolishes serfdom, and in March 1917 Nicholas II abdicates.
russland-osteuropa#sections.0.title: Rule and Politics
russland-osteuropa#sections.0.paragraphs: Kievan Rus was not a state with fixed borders but a federation of principalities ruled by members of the Rurikid dynasty. The grand prince of Kyiv stood at the top, but succession by seniority, in which brothers and nephews moved up by age, led again and again to wars between brothers. Besides the princes, their retinue, the druzhina, and the boyars carried great weight; in Novgorod the popular assembly, the veche, even elected the mayor and the archbishop and dismissed princes.

Under the rule of the Golden Horde the Russian princes remained in office but had to pay tribute and have their position confirmed by a charter from the khan, the yarlyk. Moscow rose because its princes cooperated with the Horde, bought and married into land and drew the church to their side. Ivan III and Ivan IV turned this into autocracy: the tsar claimed unlimited power granted by God, assemblies of the land such as the Zemsky Sobor advised him only at times, and the service nobility received land in return for military service.

Poland-Lithuania was constituted quite differently. In the Commonwealth of the Two Nations the nobility, the szlachta, elected the king from 1573 onwards and bound him by contracts; the parliament, the Sejm, could be paralysed by the objection of a single deputy, the liberum veto. In Russia Peter the Great replaced the boyar duma with a Senate and specialized colleges and placed the church under a state Synod; after the partitions of Poland the tsar also ruled over millions of Poles, Lithuanians, Belarusians and Ukrainians. Only the Revolution of 1905 forced him to allow an elected Duma, whose powers he nevertheless kept narrowly limited.
russland-osteuropa#sections.1.title: Society and Everyday Life
russland-osteuropa#sections.1.paragraphs: The great majority of people lived as peasants in small villages of wooden houses, growing rye, oats and flax on poor soils and enduring long winters. In Russia peasants were gradually bound to the land from the late 16th century; the law code of 1649 made serfdom hereditary. Serfs could be sold, mortgaged and handed over for military service, and in the 18th century nobles often owned hundreds or thousands of them. Many villages managed land and dues jointly in the village commune, the mir.

From the 15th century peasants and adventurers fled into the wide steppes of the south and formed the Cossack communities on the Dnieper, the Don and the Yaik. They elected their own leaders, served Polish kings and tsars as border guards, but also rose in great revolts such as those under Khmelnytsky, Stenka Razin and Pugachev. Poland-Lithuania was a multi-ethnic commonwealth in which Poles, Lithuanians, Ruthenians, Germans, Armenians, Tatars and the largest Jewish community in Europe lived; the nobility made up an estimated six to ten per cent of the population, an unusually large share.

After the partitions of Poland, Jews in the tsarist empire were allowed to live only in a western Pale of Settlement, and after the assassination of Alexander II in 1881 pogroms shook the communities, whereupon millions emigrated to America. The abolition of serfdom in 1861 made the peasants personally free but burdened them with heavy redemption payments. With industrialization at the end of the 19th century, workers' suburbs grew in St Petersburg, Moscow, Łódź and the Donets Basin, where long working hours, cramped housing and strikes shaped daily life.
russland-osteuropa#sections.2.title: Culture, Religion and Knowledge
russland-osteuropa#sections.2.paragraphs: With Volodymyr's baptism in 988, priests, icons, church architecture and the Cyrillic alphabet came to the Rus from Byzantium. Monasteries such as the Kyiv Monastery of the Caves became centres of learning where monks wrote chronicles such as the Primary Chronicle. After the fall of Constantinople in 1453 the Muscovite church saw itself as the guardian of the true faith, and in the 16th century a monk formulated the idea of Moscow as the "Third Rome". In the 17th century the reforms of Patriarch Nikon split the church, and the Old Believers were persecuted for generations.

In the western part of the region, Catholicism and the Reformation shaped intellectual life. The University of Kraków, founded in 1364 and refounded in 1400, became a centre of scholarship where Nicolaus Copernicus also studied. Francysk Skaryna of Polotsk printed biblical books in an East Slavic literary language in Prague in 1517, and in 1596 the Union of Brest placed part of the Orthodox Church in Poland-Lithuania under the authority of the pope. Centres of learning such as the Kyiv Mohyla Academy combined Orthodox tradition with Western schooling.

Peter the Great had books printed in a simplified script and founded the Academy of Sciences in St Petersburg, where scholars such as Mikhail Lomonosov worked. In the 19th century Alexander Pushkin, Leo Tolstoy and Fyodor Dostoevsky created a literature of world rank, and composers such as Mikhail Glinka and Pyotr Tchaikovsky a musical language of their own. At the same time poets such as Adam Mickiewicz and Taras Shevchenko shaped the national consciousness of Poles, Lithuanians and Ukrainians, often against the censorship and Russification policy of the tsarist empire.
russland-osteuropa#sections.3.title: Economy and Technology
